title: Redwood cost/econ discovery with Astral Quant
summary: Initial cost/unit economics discovery for Astral Quant's plan to migrate inference from on-prem GPUs to a mix of Redwood Hosted and Dedicated for real-time scoring. Focus on per-token pricing, batching and KV/prefix cache strategies, and budget constraints for peak trading hours.
next_steps: Redwood to send per-token pricing sheet and sample cost model
Customer to share 7-day sample traffic traces and prompt distribution (anonymized)
Schedule 2-hour benchmarking session on Dedicated (week of Mar 16)
Follow-up security Q&A - send SOC2 + network diagram
action_items: Maya Chen - send pricing & cost model spreadsheet - 2026-03-06
Ravi Patel - export anonymized 7-day traffic and prompt set - 2026-03-09
Diego Ramos - coordinate benchmarking env + test plan - 2026-03-12
Priya Nair - assemble security docs link and sample network diagram - 2026-03-08
transcript:
Meeting header: 2026-03-04 14:00 PDT | Duration: ~45m | Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Diego Ramos (Redwood SE), Priya Nair (Redwood Solutions); Ethan Cole, Ravi Patel, Leah Kim (Astral Quant)

[00:00] Maya Chen: hey everyone, thanks for joining on time, appreciate it. we're Maya from Redwood and with me is Diego and Priya - we'll run through cost/econ and then zoom into batching, caching and what dedicated vs hosted looks like for you.
[00:08] Ethan Cole: thanks Maya, excited. quick context - Astral Quant runs low-latency inference for scoring trading signals, about ~2k reqs/sec at peak, spikes around market open. currently self-hosted on mixed A100/NVidia clusters, looking for better economics and prod reliability.
[00:22] Diego Ramos: great, that helps. can you share current cost drivers - e.g., avg tokens per request, prompt/response length, and SLAs?
[00:30] Ravi Patel: sure - typically prompt is 120 tokens, responses average 60 tokens. we do a lot of short iterative queries too. SLA target is p95 < 150ms for top 10% flows, lower priority for batch jobs.
[00:42] Leah Kim: to add, we also have heavy cold starts for some models cause of KV cache misses - especially when backtesting different strategies.
[00:48] Maya Chen: okay makes sense. the typical levers we'll talk about are: per-token pricing (hosted), reserved capacity for dedicated (predictable throughput), and software levers like batching and prefix/KV caching to lower units. also routing policies - you can mix hosted for burst and dedicated for steady baseline.
[01:05] Ethan Cole: can you explain per-token vs dedicated economics in practice? we pay capital and ops now, want to compare.
[01:12] Diego Ramos: yeah, so for hosted API you pay per-token for input + output, and that includes the managed infra and multi-tenant optimizations. real-world throughput improvements from our continuous batching and KV cache often reduce effective tokens charged because you cache prefixes and reuse KV caches across sessions. for large steady-state throughput, Dedicated reserved capacity (monthly commit) gets you better $/token equivalent because the GPU utilization is higher and you remove multi-tenant overhead. but you take on more predictable spend.
[01:40] Ravi Patel: do you have example numbers? ballpark is fine.
[01:44] Maya Chen: high-level example - for a medium transformer, hosted list price might be $0.0009 per input token and $0.0018 per output token (example), but effective cost after batching/prefix caching and model selection could be 30-50% lower for workloads that cache well. Dedicated baseline might reduce unit CPU by another 20-40% depending on commit size and quantization profile. these are example numbers; we'll send an exact pricing sheet.
[02:06] Leah Kim: hmm that per-token is higher than what our infra cost looks like - our ops + cloud GPU amortized is roughly equivalent to $0.0006 per token today, but that doesn't count SRE overhead and pockets of low utilization.
[02:18] Diego Ramos: totally expected. one of the hidden levers is latency SLOs - if you can accept slightly higher p95 you can enable more aggressive batching which reduces per-token cost. also cold start KV miss rate matters a lot; for your workflows if many requests share prefixes we can cache and avoid recomputation.
[02:36] Ethan Cole: what about model variants - can we swap to smaller quantized variants for low-risk flows?
[02:40] Priya Nair: yes, model families + quant profiles are a big lever. we often recommend a hybrid: high-accuracy float16 or int8 for critical flows, and quantized smaller models for background scoring. Redwood Optimize suggests quant profiles per route.
[02:53] Ravi Patel: curious about batching - since you mention p95 tradeoff, how does that work with real-time scoring? we need under 150ms for market open spikes.
[03:01] Diego Ramos: continuous batching is adaptive - it forms micro-batches within a short latency window. if traffic is high (your 2k rps), batching actually reduces latency variance because it avoids queuing overhead per-request and runs big batches efficiently on GPU. when traffic is low, we fall back to low-latency single-request execution. the key is to tune batch windows and max-latency budget per route.
[03:20] Leah Kim: any concerns about tokenization or pre/post processing adding overhead? we do lots of token-level enrichment.
[03:25] Maya Chen: you'll want that pre/post processing colocated - we support edge/sidecar transforms or running transforms in your VPC for Private deployments. that keeps the Redwood runtime focused on model inference.
[03:34] Ethan Cole: ok, for Dedicated - what's the commit math? like how much reserved capacity for our 2k rps?
[03:39] Diego Ramos: depends on model and sequence length. ballpark: a single high-memory GPU (A100 equivalent) on Dedicated can serve X concurrent tokens per second (we'd show exact GPU profile in the cost model). for planning you give us QPS and token distribution and we'll size a pool. Dedicated pricing has a baseline monthly fee per GPU plus a reduced per-token charge for excess usage, or you can buy all-included tokens.
[04:00] Ravi Patel: do you have examples of customers that moved from self-host to Dedicated and saw cost parity?
[04:06] Maya Chen: yes, several quant/fin customers saw 10-30% lower total cost when you include SRE/Ops, faster time to deploy new models, and fewer outages. the split depends on utilization and how much of your stack you want Redwood to handle.
[04:18] Ethan Cole: security - we run regulated strategies. encryption at rest + KMS are musts. can Private support full air-gapped on-prem?
[04:26] Priya Nair: yes, Private supports on-prem and VPC deployments with customer-managed KMS/HSM integrations, audit logs, and role-based access. we'll send our SOC2 and sample network diagrams.
[04:36] Leah Kim: great. about benchmarking - we want to run a pilot using a representative subset during market open. what's the typical pilot plan?
[04:43] Diego Ramos: usually we do a 2-week smoke then a week-long live spike bench. step 1: get sample traffic and prompt shapes; step 2: Redwood provisions a Dedicated pool and we run a side-by-side bench (latency, throughput, cost). step 3: tune batching, cache TTLs and model variants.
[04:58] Ravi Patel: do you need raw PII or can we anonymize traces?
[05:02] Maya Chen: anonymized traces are fine; we only need token counts, timing, and example prompt shapes.
[05:07] Ethan Cole: what sort of cost savings can we expect from caching alone?
[05:11] Diego Ramos: caching depends on prefix reuse. for workflows with high prefix reuse you can see 20-60% token reduction; for low reuse, less. important to measure cold vs warm cache hit rates.
[05:23] Leah Kim: our team does backtests where prefixes vary a lot, so maybe caching won't be as effective. any other levers?
[05:29] Priya Nair: quantization + model routing (smaller models for low-risk calls), selective batching windows, and precomputed embeddings for expensive parts. also, you can route less critical flows to Hosted bursts to avoid overprovisioning Dedicated.
[05:42] Ravi Patel: how about sudden spikes - market open can be 10x baseline for 2-3 minutes. Hosted burst capacity sounds attractive but latency consistency is crucial.
[05:50] Maya Chen: we recommend hybrid: Dedicated baseline sized for 2x normal, plus Hosted bursts for extreme spikes. routing policies ensure you only send overflow to hosted; you can set fallbacks to smaller models if cost or latency thresholds hit.
[06:05] Ethan Cole: what's the SLA for Dedicated vs Hosted?
[06:08] Diego Ramos: Dedicated has SLA for uptime and latency tiers as part of the reserved contract; Hosted has public SLAs too but is multi-tenant. specifics depend on contract/enterprise tier - we'll include SLA language in follow-up.
[06:20] Leah Kim: okay good. can you walk through a simple worked example: say 2k rps average, 180 tokens total per request?
[06:27] Diego Ramos: quick math: 2k rps * 180 tokens = 360k tokens/sec = 31B tokens/day. at an example hosted price of $0.001 per token equivalent (input+output blended) that's $31k/day - but with batching, caching and model routing you could reduce effective billed tokens maybe 30% => $21-22k/day. with Dedicated, same throughput might cost 20-40% less depending on commitment and GPU efficiency plus you avoid some per-request overheads. (note: numbers illustrative).
[06:58] Ravi Patel: that daily $ figure is higher than our current raw GPU amortized number; we'd need to show total cost of ownership including SRE, reliability, and speed to iterate.
[07:07] Maya Chen: totally - that's why we do a TCO analysis. we'll include SRE hours saved and reduced incident costs in the model.
[07:14] Ethan Cole: what's the typical ramp for dedicated - lead time to spin up a pool?
[07:18] Priya Nair: dedicated pool provisioning is usually 2-5 business days depending on region and GPU type; private on-prem is longer, depends on your procurement.
[07:26] Leah Kim: fine. on governance - do you provide token-level cost visibility broken down by route/team?
[07:31] Maya Chen: yes, Redwood Console gives token-level costs by route, model, and token type; you can allocate cost centers and set quotas.
[07:39] Ravi Patel: any gotchas with model quantization and accuracy regressions? we can't afford trading drift.
[07:44] Diego Ramos: that's why Redwood Optimize includes quality monitoring and regression alerts tied to evals and prompt sets. you can rollout quantized models to a small percentage of traffic via canary and monitor quality metrics.
[07:57] Ethan Cole: okay that helps. what's required from us to get a pilot started?
[08:01] Maya Chen: we'll need anonymized traffic, a list of critical flows and SLA targets, and a short stakeholder list. then we'll propose a pilot scope and timeline.
[08:10] Ravi Patel: timeline wise, if we sign a pilot we'll aim for a benchmark mid-March.
[08:15] Priya Nair: noted - Diego will coordinate.
[08:18] Maya Chen: great. i'm going to capture next steps - Maya will send pricing & TCO template; Diego will send pilot test plan; Priya will send security docs; Ethan/Ravi will send anonymized traces.
[08:29] Ethan Cole: yep, sounds good.
[08:32] Leah Kim: quick Q - do you support per-route model pinning? like route A must always use the float16 model?
[08:37] Diego Ramos: yes, you can pin models per route and we support fallback rules to alternate models.
[08:42] Ravi Patel: and finally, billing integration - can we invoice to our procurement or do you need a committed contract?
[08:48] Maya Chen: for pilots we typically do a scoped pilot agreement; for Dedicated we'd do a reserved capacity contract with monthly invoicing. procurement details we'll handle via the sales ops team.
[08:58] Ethan Cole: ok thank you.
[09:00] Maya Chen: thanks all. we'll follow up with the materials and let's reconvene after you share traces.

[09:05] End of recording.

Notes on transcript quality: speaker labels sometimes generic; occasional transcription errors (e.g., "KV cache" sometimes appears as "K V cache"), natural speech patterns preserved.
